# kb

<!-- kb:global · generated by kb 0.6.1 -->
## Shared rules

The project section below wins where the two differ.

### Before changing: ask why, and keep one fact in one place

- `kb why <doc.md#section | path>` or `kb search <terms>` first. Each fact has one home, and the others link to it:

| Information | Home |
|---|---|
| how it is now | the topic doc |
| why, when the choice had a plausible alternative someone would propose again | a decision; otherwise a code comment or the topic doc |
| what comes next, in order; a problem with a known fix, however small | the roadmap |
| what waits on someone's answer; a problem without a chosen fix | an open question, the day it comes up |
| how agents work | AGENTS.md: rules, one line each, with a link to the doc section that explains it |
| what changed, line by line | git |

- `kb` writes decisions and questions, one file each, and builds every list when read: never edit one by hand. A change of mind is a new decision that supersedes or amends the old one. `bun kb --help` has the commands; `kb guide decisions`, the method.
- Your own memory is none of these homes: the next agent never reads it.

### While working: docs, comments and the session

- Say what the thing is and what to do; a prohibition comes with the way: "never X; use Y". Present only: the past lives in git (what) and in decisions (why).
- Comments say why; the code says what. Changed or removed code: rewrite or delete every comment and doc about it in the same commit.
- Concise: direct sentences, tables and lists when they fit. One file, one topic.
- Every turn rereads the whole conversation: `kb why` before a whole doc, a line range before a whole file, a subagent for a wide search when the harness has one.
- At the end of a task, or once the session has grown long, write what the next session needs in its home, then start fresh, or ask the person to.

### Before calling it done: evidence, kb check, the commit

- "Done", "fixed" and "passing" come after running the command in this turn and reading its output; report what it printed, and a skipped step as skipped.
- A visible change is looked at (screenshot or browser) before it is called done: tests prove only what they cover.
- Bug: reproduce it, find the cause, then fix, with a test that fails before the fix when the bug earns one. After three fixes that did not hold, question the approach.
- Review feedback: check each point against the code before applying it, and answer a wrong one with evidence. Agreement is not a reply.
- `kb check` before committing docs; `kb gen` rewrites the generated blocks.
- Conventional Commits, the description in the language the project section names; the type drives the release (`feat` minor, `fix` patch, `BREAKING CHANGE` major). `wip` never reaches the integration branch: retype or squash first.
- Commits and pull requests end at their content: no `Co-Authored-By` trailer, no "Generated with" footer.

### With the person

- A feature that replaces a process the client runs today: a portrait of that process validated with them, then a proposal in its own document, then the spec and the docs.
- A question gets an answer, the size of the question. Change something only when asked; a fix the person would obviously want, offer in one line.
- Look around what you touch: stale, duplicated, inconsistent or more complex than needed. Small and same topic: fix it in the same commit and say so; bigger: point it out and propose.
- One question at a time, with your recommendation, when the choice is genuinely theirs; otherwise pick the conventional option, say so, and go on.
- Destructive or outward-facing actions (deleting, pushing to a shared environment, sending) wait for an explicit yes.

### Roadmap

- **What comes next:** `kb roadmap`, in order. A task goes to `docs/roadmap.md`: a wish is one line under `## Later`; what comes next is a `###` item under `## Now`, in its place in the order, with its `**Done when:**` line.
- What waits on someone is an open question with `--unblocks roadmap.md#<item>`; the page keeps no blocked section.
- An item leaves the page in the commit that meets its `**Done when:**` line, and what it built lives in the topic doc; dropping one is a decision that says why. The method: `kb guide roadmap`.

### Parallel agents: wf

One orchestrator, a Claude Code session, works in the main checkout, on `main`, and leads the agents: it opens them, answers them, ships their work and tells the person. Each task gets its own git worktree, branch and agent, in a herdr pane the person watches and may step into. Never two agents in one working directory. `bun wf` covers the flow; for anything else in herdr (layout, reading a screen, focus), use `herdr` itself (`herdr --skill`).

**In a worktree: the agent**

- Work only in your worktree; commit each green step.
- The full suites belong to the ship. In your worktree, run the cheap gates (`bun wf check`, `bun kb check`, `bun run check`, `bun test`, `bun run build`); `bun wf ship` runs every gate, one ship at a time.
- Stop at what is not yours to decide, such as a business rule or the boundary with another task: ask, with the options and your recommendation. Never invent.
- A question, a choice or a plan to approve goes by `bun wf ask "<question>"` (a long one on stdin), with the options and your recommendation; then stop. With an orchestrator, it goes to the orchestrator, the person's filter: send the SendMessage it prints, and the answer comes as a message. Ask through `bun wf ask`, never with a dialog on screen (such as AskUserQuestion), which only the person can answer. Alone, `bun wf ask` calls the person: ask in your pane.
- The person may still talk to you in your pane: follow them, and say so in your report.
- Look around what you touch: stale, duplicated or misleading code and comments. Say what you found.
- Before touching what another worktree touches (`bun wf status` lists them), tell its agent: `bun wf tell <name> "<text>"` prints the SendMessage that carries it to the agent's session; send it.
- Finish with `bun wf report`, the report on stdin: the commits; the commands you ran and what they printed; what to look at; open questions, with options and your recommendation; what you noticed around. It prints the message that tells the orchestrator (in Claude Code, SendMessage to its session): send it, then stop.
- The report fits the change. A small change gets a short one: the commits, the last lines of the gates, what to look at. Leave out a section with nothing to say.
- One task, one session: a follow-up on your task continues here; a new task, whoever brings it, gets its own worktree and agent, never this session. A batch of small fixes is one task: one commit per fix, one report. A fix that turns out bigger than the task says goes by `bun wf ask`, and leaves the batch for a task of its own.
- Never merge, push or close the worktree: the orchestrator ships it.

**In the main checkout: the orchestrator**

- You split the work and open the agents, without asking the person. One task, one worktree, one agent the person can watch: `bun wf spawn <name> --task <file>`, tool upgrades included (a handoff from another tool, such as kb's upgrade steps, becomes the task file). A follow-up on a task goes to its agent (`bun wf tell`, or `bun wf resume` when it is gone); a new task gets a new agent, never the session of another task. Never open a worktree by hand or edit in one: its agent does the work, and you read, check and ship it. `bun wf status` marks a worktree with no agent.
- Small fixes go in batches. A fix is small when its cause and place are known and fit in one line, and it touches no business rule and nothing the project's own section of this file marks as sensitive. A batch is one task: 2 to 4 small fixes, listed in one task file, for one worktree and one agent, with one commit per fix and one report. A fix that turns out bigger comes back by `bun wf ask` and leaves the batch for a task of its own.
- Keep `bun wf watch` running as your harness's own background command (in Claude Code, the Bash tool with `run_in_background`): when it returns, start it again first, then act on what it returned. Never run it with `&`, `nohup` or `disown`, nor with its output discarded: nobody would read what it delivers, so `watch` refuses. One watch runs per repository; a new one replaces the old, which then says not to start it again. Run `bun wf ship` the same way: its gates take minutes.
- Each return of `bun wf watch` reads your whole conversation again: keep it lean. Read a report narrowly, and a large diff by parts (`--stat` first, then one file's diff), and send wide reading to a subagent when your harness has one.
- A message to an agent goes by `bun wf tell <name> "<text>"`, which prints the SendMessage that carries it to the agent's session: send it. Never type into an agent's pane: the person may be typing there.
- You are the person's filter. An agent's question (`bun wf watch` returns it, the agent's message brings it) is yours: answer what exists settles (`kb why`, the decisions, the docs, the person's earlier choices) with `bun wf tell <name> "<answer>"`, naming the basis; record a decision (`kb decision new`) when someone could later ask "why?"; and tell the person what you decided and why.
- Bring to the person only a product question nothing settles, a permission, a push or a publish, or anything destructive or outward; relay their answer with `bun wf tell`. A question left unanswered for ten minutes calls the person.
- A dialog on an agent's screen (a tool permission, an approval) is the person's: the herdr plugin has called them, and `bun wf watch` calls again every five minutes while it waits. Never press it, nor type in the agent's pane.
- A report is a claim, and your review adds what the gates cannot: read the diff (`git diff main...worktree/<name>`), whole when it is small, `--stat` first and then one file at a time when it is large, and look at what changed on screen. Leave the gates to `bun wf ship`, which runs every one before the fast-forward, the cheap first, and stops at the first that fails; never rerun them before it.
- A test that fails with no cause in the change goes to quarantine, never three reruns, and only with proof: it fails on `main` without the change too, or passes alone and fails only under load. Then tell the agent (`bun wf tell <name>`) to skip it and name it as an open question in its report, with the proof, and ship again without it. A test that fails only with the change is a bug to fix.
- `bun wf ship <name>` brings `main` in, prepares the worktree, runs every gate (`bun wf check`, `bun kb check`, `bun run check`, `bun test`, `bun run build`), fast-forwards `main` to the tested commit and closes the worktree. `bun wf close <name>` abandons one. Never close a worktree with `$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID`: in the main checkout it names the main checkout's workspace.
- A fresh session takes over after a round of tasks ships, or once this one has grown long. The state lives outside the conversation: `bun wf status`, the reports and the project's records (the decisions by `kb decision new`, the roadmap, the open questions by `kb question add`). Write there first what lives only in the conversation, such as an answer you gave an agent that should outlast it, or a yes the person still owes; then tell the person this session is ready to hand over (in Claude Code, `/clear`). The new session reads `bun wf status` and starts `bun wf watch` again.
- Pushing to a shared environment waits for the person's yes.

**Alone in a worktree**, with no orchestrator: you are both. `bun wf ask` calls the person, and you finish with `bun wf ship` from the worktree.
<!-- /wf:rules -->

## This project

- `bun kb` runs this repo's source (`src/cli.ts`), so `bun kb gen` writes the shared block from `templates/agents/` as they stand.
- The topic docs are README.md and the guides in `guides/`, which `kb guide` prints: outside the docs folder, without frontmatter; a reference to them starts at the repo root (`--lives-in /README.md#config`). `docs/` holds the roadmap (`docs/roadmap.md`), the decisions and the open questions.
- Commit descriptions are in English.
- This repository and the `@tekne/kb` package are public: docs, decisions, comments, tests and commits name no other project of the studio and none of its details (names, paths, people, data). Describe the case by its shape instead: "a project whose E2E and browser suites take 4 minutes".
